newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Key facts on Bolivia's elections today.
newsitem.headline: Key facts on Bolivia's elections today.

text.p: Bolivians vote for president on Sunday in elections which are likely to produce no clear winner, leaving the country's Congress to choose the next ruler of the landlocked Andean nation.
The three leading candidates are expected to maintain the country's free market-oriented economic policy, introduced in 1985 to tame runaway inflation.

Twelve years later, the country's annual inflation has sunk to single digits. Sweeping reforms have slimmed the government after its sell-off of major state companies, including the oil, telephone and electricity firms.

But Bolivia remains one of Latin America's poorest countries. Though its average annual gross domestic product growth has run at a clip of four percent in recent years, per capita income is only around $850.
The question now is whether the government to be elected will preserve or modify the ambitious privatization program of outgoing President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada.
He is slated to hand over power to a new president on August 6. The new administration will last five years, up from the current four years under a 1995 constitutional amendment.

To be elected president, a candidate must win more than 50 percent of the vote. If the poll fails to produce a winner, a likely scenario in this election, Congress will vote on the two leading candidates.
Here are other facts about the election:
-- Bolivians will vote for president, vice president, 27 senators and 130 deputies.

-- Polls open at 0800 local time/0800 EDT/1200 GMT and close at 1800 local time/1800 EDT/2200 GMT. Some 3.3 million Bolivians are eligible to vote, including youths aged between 18-21 who will be casting their ballots for the first time in a presidential election.

-- The candidates are Gen. Hugo Banzer, former military ruler between 1971-1978 of the Nationalist Democratic Action; Jaime Paz Zamora, former president between 1989-1993 of the Revolutionary Left Movement; Juan Carlos Duran, top candidate of the ruling center-right Nationalist Revolutionary Movement; and Ivo Kuljis of the populist Solidarity Civic Union.
-- Opinion polls show Banzer leading the pack with between 25-30 percent support, followed by Paz Zamora with 15-20 percent, and Duran in third place, slightly ahead of Kuljis.
-- Exit polls and forecasts will be released after polling stations close at 1800 local time/1800 EDT/2200 GMT.
Following are key facts about the country:
-- Size: 1,098,581 sq km (424,195 sq miles).
-- Population: 7.9 million, of whom over half are pure Quechua and Aymara Indians with the rest of mixed Indian or Spanish descent, or Europeans.
-- Capital: Sucre (population 150,000).
-- Government seat: La Paz (population 1.2 million).
-- Official language: Spanish.
-- Religion: 95 percent Catholic.
-- Illiteracy rate: 37 percent.
-- Main exports: zinc, gold, hydrocarbons, soybeans, wood (total 1996 exports $1.3 billion)."
-- Currency: Boliviano. Trades at 5.22 per dolar.
-- Per capita income: U.S. $850.
-- Inflation rate in 1996: 7.95 percent.
-- Foreign debt: $4.52 billion at end-1996.
-- Drugs: Bolivia has approximately 45,000 hectares of coca fields, of which only 12,000 are legally authorized to provide raw leaves for chewing, a longtime practice of Bolivia's highland Indians.
The country is considered to be the second world producer of coca leaves, after Peru, and the third largest producer of cocaine after Peru and Colombia.
